description: Why people committed crimes across 1,500 years — poverty, religion, industry and technology.
content_html:
Why Do People Commit Crime?

The causes of crime have never been simple. Across 1,500 years of British history, what drove people to break the law reflected the pressures of their age — hunger and poverty, religious conflict, economic dislocation and, more recently, the temptations and tools of the modern world. Understanding the causes of crime is not just about judging wrongdoers; it is about understanding the society that produced them.

Medieval Poverty and Survival Crime

In the medieval era, the great majority of people lived on the edge of subsistence. A failed harvest could tip a family from poverty into starvation within months. Petty theft — stealing food, livestock or tools — was overwhelmingly the most common crime, and much of it was driven simply by hunger. Famine years, such as the Great Famine of 1315–1322, saw theft rates rise sharply across England as communities struggled to survive. Warfare compounded the problem: armies marching through the countryside looted supplies and left devastated villages in their wake, pushing more people into desperate criminality.

Key Fact

The two dominant causes of crime in the medieval era were poverty — particularly famine and harvest failure — and the disruption caused by warfare. Petty theft of food and livestock was by far the most common offence.

Tudor Inflation and Economic Pressure

The sixteenth century brought new economic stresses. A dramatic rise in population — England’s population roughly doubled between 1500 and 1600 — pushed up the price of food and land. Wages, however, failed to keep pace, leaving the poor worse off in real terms. This period of inflation created widespread hardship. Many landlords also converted arable land to sheep pasture, requiring fewer labourers and driving thousands off the land. The displaced and unemployed drifted to towns, where they were feared as potential criminals. Parliament responded with a series of Poor Laws, but these created their own problem: to be in the wrong place without work was itself made a crime through vagrancy legislation.

The Protestant Reformation, beginning in England during Henry VIII’s reign in the 1530s, made religious belief a political act. Catholics who refused to attend the new Protestant church services faced recusancy fines and, at times, execution. Conversely, under Mary I (1553–1558), Protestants were burned as heretics. The same actions — attending a particular form of worship, owning a forbidden Bible translation, harbouring a priest — were crimes under one regime but virtuous acts under another.

Fears of witchcraft also intensified during this period. Economic hardship, religious anxiety and superstition combined to produce witch panics, particularly in the 1640s when Matthew Hopkins operated as Witchfinder General in East Anglia. Historians estimate that around 300 people were executed as witches in England between 1560 and 1680. These prosecutions reflected social tensions as much as genuine belief in the supernatural.

Industrialisation and Urbanisation

The Industrial Revolution, gathering pace from the 1760s onwards, transformed both the nature and the scale of crime. Rapid urbanisation created overcrowded cities where poverty was concentrated and traditional community controls broke down. In pre-industrial villages, everyone knew their neighbours; anonymous city life made it far easier to commit crime and escape detection. Towns such as Manchester, Birmingham and Leeds grew at astonishing speed: Manchester’s population rose from around 25,000 in 1772 to over 300,000 by 1850.

Key Fact

Rapid urban growth in the nineteenth century concentrated poverty, created anonymous communities and overwhelmed the old parish-based systems of law enforcement. These conditions made certain crimes — particularly pick-pocketing, prostitution and street robbery — far easier to commit than they had been in rural communities.

The disruption of traditional livelihoods also created collective crimes driven by desperation. The Luddite movement (1811–1813) saw framework knitters smash textile machinery in the Midlands and North of England — their livelihoods threatened by mechanisation. The Swing Riots of 1830 involved agricultural labourers destroying threshing machines across the south of England. These acts of disorder were crimes in law, but to participants they were legitimate protests against economic injustice. Both movements were suppressed with military force, with transportation and execution used as deterrents.

Twentieth-Century Pressures

In the twentieth and twenty-first centuries new causes emerged. The rise of the motor car created entirely new categories of crime — speeding, drink-driving and vehicle theft. Consumer society generated new targets for property crime and fraud. The two World Wars disrupted social norms and left many ex-servicemen traumatised, contributing to rises in violent crime in the 1920s and 1940s. Drug-related crime grew from the 1960s onwards as heroin, cannabis and later cocaine became more widely available. More recently, the internet has produced cybercrime — fraud, identity theft and hacking — on a scale impossible for earlier generations to have imagined.

Throughout all these periods, continuities exist alongside the changes. Poverty has been a constant driver of crime from Anglo-Saxon England to the present day. Social exclusion, the absence of legitimate opportunity and the perception that the law serves the powerful have recurred as themes across every era. What changes is the form that crime takes, not the underlying human pressures that produce it.
exam_tip_html: For the 16-mark thematic change essay on causes of crime, you must cover all three eras: medieval, early modern (sixteenth–seventeenth centuries) and modern (nineteenth century onwards). A common mistake is spending too long on one era and neglecting the others — examiners expect evidence from each period. Show change (new causes emerging) but also continuity (poverty appears in every era). For the 8-mark ‘Explain Change’ question, name a specific cause, explain why it changed, and link it to the wider context of the era.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Causes of crime have changed across the eras but poverty is a constant thread — from medieval famine-theft to industrial-era destitution to modern drug-related crime.
  • The sixteenth and seventeenth centuries added new causes: religious change (heresy, recusancy, witchcraft panics) and Tudor inflation displacing agricultural workers into vagrancy.
  • Industrialisation and urbanisation from the 1760s created anonymous cities where traditional controls broke down, producing new crimes driven by poverty, collective protest and, eventually, technology.

practice_questions.text: Describe one reason why poverty caused crime in medieval England.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Students should identify a specific mechanism: e.g. harvest failure drove people to steal food or livestock; famine years such as 1315-1322 created widespread desperation; warfare disrupted food supply and pushed communities into survival crime. A simple identification (1 mark); development with context or example (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the impact of religious change on crime in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail). Feature 1: Religious legislation created new crimes — Catholics who refused to attend Protestant services were guilty of recusancy, and priests risked execution. Feature 2: Witchcraft fears produced prosecution waves — the Witchcraft Act of 1563 made witchcraft a capital offence, and during the 1640s Matthew Hopkins prosecuted hundreds in East Anglia. Other valid features: Protestant heretics burned under Mary I; possession of forbidden devotional materials became criminal.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the increase in crime during the Industrial Revolution.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: Names a cause (e.g. urbanisation) without explanation. Developing: Identifies urbanisation and notes it created overcrowded cities. Secure: Explains how anonymity of city life broke down traditional community controls, making crime easier to commit and harder to detect; may add specific detail (Manchester population growth, pick-pocketing and street robbery rising). Mastering: Sustains analytical explanation linking rapid urbanisation to the breakdown of parish-based enforcement, uses specific evidence (population figures, types of crime), and connects to the wider context of industrialisation displacing rural workers.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Luddite movement (1811-1813) as evidence of a cause of crime.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: Identifies Luddites smashed machinery. Developing: Explains economic threat to framework knitters from mechanisation. Secure: Analyses significance at the time (collective response to livelihood destruction; treated as capital crime by the state) and connects to a wider cause (industrial displacement as a driver of disorder). Mastering: Sustains analysis of significance both at the time and over time; evaluates whether collective industrial crime represents continuity with earlier survival crime or a new phenomenon unique to industrialisation; reaches a substantiated judgement.

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree that poverty was the main cause of crime in Britain between c.500 and the present day?
Give reasons for your answer. You should refer to different periods in your response.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments supporting poverty as the main cause: medieval famine-theft; Tudor inflation and displacement; urban destitution driving pick-pocketing and prostitution; twentieth-century drug crime linked to deprivation. Arguments for other causes: religious change (Reformation, witchcraft) creating entirely new categories of crime; industrialisation and mechanisation producing collective protest crime; twentieth-century technology enabling cybercrime regardless of poverty. Emerging: One-sided or superficial. Developing: Both sides noted but not sustained. Secure: Clear argument with evidence from at least two eras; some weighing. Mastering: Sustained argument across all three eras, weighs poverty against other causes with specific evidence, reaches a justified overall conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of twentieth-century causes of crime that were not present in earlier centuries.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per feature. Feature 1: Motor vehicles created new crime categories — speeding, drink-driving and car theft emerged only after the spread of the motor car from the early twentieth century. Feature 2: Cybercrime (fraud, identity theft, hacking) emerged from the late twentieth century as internet use became universal, enabling crime on a global scale impossible in earlier eras. Other valid features: drug-related crime growing from the 1960s; terrorism by organisations using modern communications.

knowledge_checks.q: What was the most common crime in medieval England?
options: Petty theft, especially of food and livestock

knowledge_checks.q: Which economic change in the sixteenth century pushed many agricultural workers off the land and into vagrancy?
options: The closure of monasteries and loss of charity
Landlords converting arable land to sheep pasture
The Black Death reducing the workforce
The construction of the railway network

knowledge_checks.q: The _____ of 1563 made witchcraft a capital offence in England.
The rapid growth of cities during the Industrial Revolution broke down traditional _____ controls, making crime easier to commit and harder to detect.
Match each period to the new cause of crime it introduced:

flashcard_questions.q: What was the most common crime in medieval England and what drove it?
flashcard_questions.a: Petty theft of food and livestock, driven primarily by poverty and harvest failure.

flashcard_questions.q: The Great Famine of 1315-1322 caused theft rates to rise. Why?
flashcard_questions.a: Crop failures pushed communities to starvation, leaving theft as the only means of survival.

flashcard_questions.q: How did the Reformation create new crimes in the sixteenth century?
flashcard_questions.a: Attending the wrong church or harbouring a priest became criminal under recusancy laws.
The offence of failing to attend Church of England services, punishable by fine under Elizabethan law.

flashcard_questions.q: Who was Matthew Hopkins and what role did he play in seventeenth-century crime?
flashcard_questions.a: Witchfinder General in East Anglia in the 1640s who prosecuted hundreds for witchcraft.

flashcard_questions.q: How did Tudor inflation contribute to crime?
flashcard_questions.a: Rising food prices and enclosure of land left many unemployed and destitute, driving theft and vagrancy.

flashcard_questions.q: The Luddite movement (1811-1813) is an example of crime caused by what?
flashcard_questions.a: Industrial displacement — framework knitters smashed machinery that threatened their livelihoods.

flashcard_questions.q: The Swing Riots of 1830 involved agricultural labourers doing what, and why?
flashcard_questions.a: Destroying threshing machines to protest against mechanisation threatening their employment.

flashcard_questions.q: How did urbanisation in the nineteenth century encourage crime?
flashcard_questions.a: Overcrowded, anonymous cities broke down community controls, making crime easier to commit.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one new category of crime created by the motor car in the twentieth century.
flashcard_questions.a: Drink-driving (also valid: speeding or vehicle theft).
Criminal activity using computers or the internet, such as fraud, hacking or identity theft.

flashcard_questions.q: Which cause of crime is a continuous thread from the medieval era to the present day?
flashcard_questions.a: Poverty — it drives crime in every era, though the form of crime changes.

glossary_terms.definition: The underlying reasons why individuals or groups break the law at a particular time.
The period from roughly 500 to 1500 CE, sometimes called the Middle Ages.
A sustained rise in prices that reduces the purchasing power of wages.
The offence of failing to attend Church of England services, punishable by fine under Elizabethan law.
The practice of diabolism or the dark arts, made a capital offence in England by the Witchcraft Act of 1563.
Criminal activity carried out using computers or the internet, such as fraud, hacking or the spread of illegal content.
